key_finding: A nudge that shrouded the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce debt, and actually reduced autopay enrollment and increased missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment on live credit-card accounts with six-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Direct consumer-financial evidence that changing enrollment defaults can shift nominal enrollment without improving the underlying financial outcome, and can even backfire via missed payments — the exact 'vanity enrollment' risk the support team is flagging for round-up defaults.
limitations: credit-card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
does not test opt-out vs active-choice enrollment structures directly
relevance_reason: Consumer, self-directed, liquid financial-product field experiment that contradicts the premise that shifting defaults reliably improves the outcome people care about.

key_finding: State-of-the-art narrative synthesis of DC plan design, covering short- and long-term effects of automatic enrollment and defaults, including potential negative effects on participant engagement.
why_it_matters: Gives an up-to-date map of what the retirement-plan default literature currently says about engagement costs, useful as background even though its intermediary (employer) doesn't map onto our app.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer self-directed app
narrative overview rather than a quantified synthesis
relevance_reason: Recent overview of the closest analogous literature (employer defaults) flagged for the engagement-cost question, but off-domain relative to a consumer app.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces behavioral inertia — low contribution rates, non-engagement, and account churn — undermining welfare gains from participation alone.
why_it_matters: States explicitly the support team's counter-argument (passive enrollees don't engage and churn), which is exactly the trade-off the brief asks us to weigh before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: US employer retirement system, not consumer liquid savings
no quantitative effect sizes given
relevance_reason: Directly voices and reviews evidence for the disengagement/passivity risk of opt-out defaults that the brief needs evaluated.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when defaults do or do not produce lasting ('downstream') behavior change, identifying time course, prior preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
methodology: Conceptual synthesis and research agenda, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a framework for predicting when our opt-out default will or won't persist past sign-up — directly shapes what to measure (retention, disengagement) and how to interpret it, rather than dictating the design itself.
limitations: theoretical/synthesis paper, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: General consumer choice-architecture synthesis on persistence of default effects, matching the brief's central open question about whether enrollment lift survives past onboarding.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug use, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option, even with random assignment.
methodology: Three natural experiments including random assignment to default options in a large administrative dataset.
why_it_matters: Strong causal evidence that passivity toward defaults is not simply low engagement but structural inattention — relevant to interpreting whether opt-out enrollment reflects genuine preference or inertia in our product.
limitations: health-insurance/drug-plan setting, not financial savings
low-income beneficiary population differs from a general banking-app user base
relevance_reason: Rigorous individual-choice default study with an active-choice comparison, useful analogy for how sticky opt-out defaults are even against high stakes.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of auto-escalation defaults survive the first escalation date.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans accounting for job separation, balance withdrawal, and opt-out from auto-escalation.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: default-driven enrollment gains shrink sharply once turnover, withdrawal, and later opt-out are accounted for — exactly the persistence question the brief asks about.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated context differs from a self-service banking app
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults durably raise saving, with real effect sizes at multiple horizons.

key_finding: Nationwide German auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most individuals subsequently actively opt out, with the default effect strongest among those low on enrollment-status knowledge.
methodology: Administrative and survey data around a nationwide policy introduction of automatic pension enrollment.
why_it_matters: Shows a large headline enrollment effect coexisting with widespread active opt-out, illustrating exactly the gap between nominal enrollment and durable participation the brief is worried about.
limitations: public pension system, government/employer-mediated
abstract does not report post-opt-out savings amounts
relevance_reason: Large, recent default-effect estimate with an opt-out/knowledge heterogeneity angle relevant to who is helped or hurt.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's short-run (12-month) gains in participation and contributions attenuate substantially by 36 months, though it does reduce inequality in savings; a life-cycle model fits this with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Quantifies exactly how much the default 'enrollment win' fades over 1–3 years, giving a concrete benchmark for judging whether an opt-out round-up feature's enrollment numbers will hold up at 6–12 months.
limitations: employer-mediated retirement plans, not a consumer banking app
liquidity and stakes differ greatly from small round-up sums
relevance_reason: Directly measures the persistence-of-default-effect question central to the brief, with a multi-horizon comparison.

key_finding: Across three experiments (including n=4207 across five European countries), default nudges shift risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes, but they also lower how trustworthy/honest the advice is perceived to be, especially when the targeted individual refuses the default; framing of the default presentation (e.g., asking amount to invest vs. amount to keep safe) produces smaller but real anchoring shifts.
methodology: Three experiments including a large representative multi-country European sample; between-subjects manipulation of default presence and framing.
why_it_matters: Directly informs both open decisions: it shows preset defaults anchor chosen amounts, and quantifies the reputational/manipulation cost of an unwanted default being applied — the EU dark-pattern risk the brief flags for choosing among opt-in/opt-out/active-choice designs.
limitations: wealth-manager advisory context rather than a purely self-service app
risk-allocation decisions, not round-up multipliers specifically
relevance_reason: European, consumer-financial experimental evidence on anchoring by presented defaults and on when a default is perceived as manipulative — squarely the questions behind the level and entry-mode decisions.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment pushed 401(k) participation above 85%, but roughly 80% of participants accepted both the default savings rate (2-3%) and default conservative fund, with half still at the default after three years, largely offsetting participation gains against low default anchoring.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracked over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors most enrollees onto it for years — the strongest historical evidence for why choosing which multiplier (1x/2x/5x) to pre-select matters as much as the entry mode.
limitations: pre-2010s employer 401(k) data, predates app-based fintech and EU consumer-protection climate
employer-mediated trust context does not transfer
relevance_reason: The foundational anchoring-on-default-level study the newer literature responds to; directly relevant to the level decision despite being off-domain for the consumer-app setting.

key_finding: In 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out effort cost together — removing either friction alone does not sustain adherence — and adding an intermediate preset option (15% alongside 20/25/30%) captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain from full menu redesign.
methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6M transaction records plus an independent stated-preference survey identifying true preferences.
why_it_matters: Gives a transferable method for the multiplier-level decision: it separates 'people pick the preset because changing it is annoying' from 'people pick the preset because it matches their preference,' and shows how adding one well-chosen extra preset level can capture most of the welfare gain — directly usable for deciding between a 1x/2x/5x menu and an empty field.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a savings product
one-off payment context, not a persistent enrollment/withdrawal decision
relevance_reason: Names an explicit transferable method (deviation-cost vs. opt-out-cost decomposition and preset-menu design) for structuring the multiplier-level decision, in a consumer self-directed opt-out setting.

key_finding: An opt-in liquid short-term savings program at five UK firms saw very low take-up (≤0.7% of eligible employees ever activated) but strong retention among those who did — 96% still held a balance and 87% received a payroll contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study tracking employee accounts for up to 12 months following program launch.
why_it_matters: The closest analog to our exact liquid, short-term product: shows opt-in for this kind of account produces near-zero enrollment but excellent persistence among enrollees, directly bearing on whether opt-in alone is viable for a round-up feature.
limitations: employer payroll-mediated enrollment, not a self-service banking app
no opt-out or active-choice arm to compare against
relevance_reason: Directly on-topic for liquid, short-term consumer savings persistence, though the employer-intermediary mechanism limits transfer to the entry-mode decision.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish savings records, automatic (passive) employer contributions raised wealth accumulation substantially, while tax subsidies requiring active choice induced only $0.01 of extra saving per $1 spent, because ~85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies and only ~15% are wealthier, financially sophisticated 'active savers.'
methodology: Population-wide administrative panel data (41M observations) from Denmark, quasi-experimental variation in savings policies.
why_it_matters: The foundational large-scale evidence that automatic/passive mechanisms reach a population that active-choice mechanisms systematically miss, and that the people missed are the less financially sophisticated — central to the brief's distributional 'who is helped, who is hurt' question.
limitations: employer/tax-subsidized retirement savings context, not a self-directed banking app
dataset from 2014, predates the app-based fintech and EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: The classic active-vs-passive savings study underlying the modern default-effect literature, directly bearing on the active-choice-vs-default trade-off and distributional heterogeneity.

key_finding: Field experiments show that 'enhanced active choice' — active choice framed to highlight the losses of the non-preferred option — can motivate behavior change and is proposed as a complement to, or substitute for, automatic enrollment.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and a novel 'enhanced active choice' variant; abstract-only, no effect sizes given.
why_it_matters: Directly speaks to the entry-design decision: it offers a tested, specific variant of active choice (loss-framed) that could outperform plain active choice or opt-out without the passive-enrollment disengagement risk the support team worries about — a concrete design option worth prototyping for onboarding.
limitations: setting is medication adherence/health decisions, not consumer financial products
no quantitative effect sizes reported in the abstract
does not measure amount saved or persistence over months
relevance_reason: Introduces and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' as an explicit alternative to opt-out enrollment, the exact entry-design technique the brief is deciding between, with an explicit link to savings/opt-out policy contexts.

key_finding: A broad overview of household financial behavior and the interventions (education, peer effects, product design, choice architecture, and price/quantity nudges) firms and governments use to shape it, synthesizing where behavioral patterns deviate from the classical model.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter covering consumption-savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance; abstract-only, no effect sizes given.
why_it_matters: Frames the whole choice-architecture toolkit (including defaults and product design) in a consumer household-finance setting rather than an employer-plan one, giving the team a map of which levers (not just opt-out defaults) are evidenced to matter for self-directed financial decisions like the round-up feature.
limitations: broad survey rather than a focused study of enrollment defaults
no quantitative effect sizes in the abstract
does not isolate active-choice vs opt-out vs opt-in comparisons specifically
relevance_reason: A high-quality, consumer-setting (not employer-plan) synthesis of behavioral household finance that covers defaults, choice architecture, and product design — the exact intervention category the brief is deciding on.
